title: Vending Machine Coin Mixes
story: An old station vending machine gives no change, so you must pay the exact price. A drink costs 30 cents and the machine takes 5, 10 and 25 cent coins: six 5s, three 10s, a 25 and a 5, and so on.
Order does not matter: a 25 then a 5 is the same handful as a 5 then a 25. You want the number of different handfuls.
task: Write countMixes(coins, price). coins lists the accepted coin values, and you have as many of each as you need. Return how many different handfuls add up to exactly price. Two handfuls are the same if they contain the same number of each coin value.
A price of 0 has exactly one handful: no coins at all. If the price cannot be paid, return 0.

examples.explanation: The handfuls are: six 5s; one 10 and four 5s; two 10s and two 5s; three 10s; one 25 and one 5. That is 5.
Only 2 + 2 + 3 works. Counting orders would give 3 (2-2-3, 2-3-2, 3-2-2), but those are all the same handful.

hints: In the second example, a careless count finds 3 answers for one handful by counting 2-2-3 and 3-2-2 separately. How can each handful be built in only one order?
Decide coin types one at a time in a fixed order: how many 5s, then how many 10s, then how many 25s. Each handful then has one way to be built.
Keep an array ways[a] = number of handfuls that pay exactly a using only the coin types handled so far. Start with ways[0] = 1 and zeros elsewhere. How does adding one new coin type c change it?

For each coin type c (outer loop), go through amounts a from c up to price (inner loop): ways[a] += ways[a - c]. Going upward lets a handful use the new coin several times. Swapping the loops counts orders instead of handfuls.
bruteForce: Recursively choose how many of each coin to use and count the choices that hit the price. With a 1-cent coin and many coin types, there can be trillions of handfuls, and the recursion visits every one.
The same subquestion, like "how many ways to pay 40 cents with only 5s and 10s", comes up again and again. A table answers each one once.

* @return {number} number of different handfuls (order does not matter)

walkthrough: The danger is counting one handful in several orders, so bring in coin types one by one. After each coin type, ways[a] counts handfuls for a made only from the types so far, and each handful is built exactly one way.
• At the start the array is [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0], because only a price of 0 can be paid, with no coins.
• Add 2s. For a = 2..7, ways[a] += ways[a - 2], which gives [1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0]. Each even amount can be paid with 2s only, in exactly one way.
• Add 3s. a = 3: += ways[0] → 1. a = 4: += ways[1] → 1. a = 5: += ways[2] → 1. a = 6: += ways[3], which is already 1 → 2. a = 7: += ways[4] → 1.
Result: ways[7] = 1 (2 + 2 + 3), and ways[6] = 2 (2 + 2 + 2 and 3 + 3). Going upward allowed 3 + 3: ways[3] already included one 3 when ways[6] read it.
solution.timeWhy: Each of the k coin types needs one pass over the amounts from 0 to the price.
solution.spaceWhy: The table stores one count for each amount from 0 to the price.
solution.takeaway: To count combinations rather than orderings, put the items in the outer loop and the totals in the inner loop. Each combination is then built in one fixed order. Swap the loops and you count sequences instead.
